item.title: ADHD and Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria
item.description:
I'd just heard of RSD for the first time a couple of days ago.
Two words. "No worries." And an ADHD brain is already spiraling: is she mad at me? Does she still want me around? On the Mel Robbins Podcast, psychiatrist and ADHD specialist Dr. Sasha Hamdani pulled up her own texts with Mel to show what Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria looks like from the inside. A neutral reply comes in. Her brain attaches uncertainty to it, reads it as a verdict on her self-worth, and floods with alarm. Then come the patterns: chew on it for hours, or over-check ("just making sure we're cool"), or decide the friendship is over before anyone can leave first. "That has been my trajectory in my 20s with relationships," she says. Here is what the research actually says. RSD is not an official diagnosis. The term comes from psychiatrist William Dodson, who reported that nearly every ADHD patient he asked, around 99 percent, recognized the experience. That number is a clinical observation, not a measured prevalence. What IS measured: emotion dysregulation affects an estimated 30 to 70 percent of adults with ADHD (Shaw et al., American Journal of Psychiatry), and a 2023 systematic review argues it belongs among ADHD's core symptoms. The feeling is real. The science around it is still young, and the diagnostic manuals have not caught up. What helps, per clinicians: name it while it is happening ("this is my rejection alarm"), delay the reply until the wave passes, ask what else the message could mean, and treat the underlying ADHD. The spiral gets shorter when it has a name. The text was never the threat. The alarm was in the wiring. Video: Mel Robbins (The Mel Robbins Podcast) ft. Dr. Sasha Hamdani (@thepsychdoctormd)

item.title: In case you have connected the dots yet, with today’s 3.000 km hit, Ukraine put russia’s oil fields on notice. The fields are between 2,000 to 3,000 kms from the frontline. Think Gulf War 1991. Thank you for your attention to this matter
item.description:
On September 9, units of the Deep Strike component of the Ukrainian SOF successfully struck two major gas condensate processing facilities — the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants.
The facilities play a critical role in russia’s gas condensate industry, processing significant volumes of condensate extracted from fields across the Yamal region. The Novy Urengoy Gas Condensate Processing Plant has a designed capacity of 19.5 million tonnes of feedstock per year, while the Purovsky Gas Processing Plant processed 13.4 million tonnes of gas condensate in 2025. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces continue to deliver long-range sanctions against Russia, degrading its ability to wage its war of aggression. Slava Ukraïni
